children: With less than 15 days left for Samvat 2083 to begin, Indian equities are entering the new Hindu financial year on a distinctly bearish note, marked by heightened volatility, weak investor sentiment and little conviction that markets have found a durable bottom.

Samvat 2082 is shaping up to be the worst Samvat year for investors since Prime Minister Narendra Modi assumed office in 2014. The Nifty is down around 13 per cent so far in the current Samvat year, a far steeper decline than the previous worst-performing Samvat of 2078 (3 November 2021 to 21 October 2022), when the benchmark index fell 1.4 per cent amid aggressive global interest-rate hikes, soaring inflation and the fallout from the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

The sharp correction stands in contrast to the strong gains investors have enjoyed over much of the past decade. Samvat 2080 delivered returns of 24.6 per cent, while Samvat 2077 saw a spectacular 40.2 per cent rally on the back of post-pandemic recovery and abundant global liquidity. Between Samvat 2071 to 2081, the market have registered an average return of 12 per cent.

“The current market phase is unusual because it lacks the normal signs of a turnaround that often emerge before a new Samvat begins, said Anand James, Chief Market Strategist at Geojit Financial Services. “This is the first time we are entering a Samvat period without visible signs of bottoming out,” James said.

He noted that the Nifty has slipped back to levels seen in May 2026 while India VIX has climbed above 30, signalling elevated uncertainty among traders. Beneath the surface, the damage has been even more severe.
“The mood is quite negative, though it is not fully reflected in the Nifty because a few heavyweight stocks, particularly in IT and PSU banking, have held up the benchmark,” he said.

While small-cap stocks have corrected far more sharply than frontline indices, indicating broader weakness across the market, investors continue to struggle to identify fresh triggers capable of reigniting risk appetite.

Rising crude oil prices, inching towards $120 per barrel, inflation concerns, geopolitical risks and signs of slowing liquidity have all contributed to the cautious mood. While funds locked in recent IPOs may eventually return to secondary markets, marketmen believe the weakness cannot be explained by liquidity factors alone.
“When money becomes dearer, money will look at growth. It won’t go to a market just for safety, they’ll go for growth,” said Dinshaw Irani, MD & CEO, Helios Capital Asset Management.
Meanwhile, drawing comparisons with 2019, before the pandemic-led bull run, the current conditions resemble a prolonged phase of consolidation rather than the beginning of a new structural uptrend.
“We are going into the crucial Samvat period with a sense of caution,” James said, warning that further downside cannot be ruled out despite markets trading near important support levels.

Irani believes India’s structural growth story remains intact despite near-term volatility. “Markets will always face phases of volatility, but India’s structural growth drivers remain stronger than ever. We believe investors should look beyond the noise and focus on companies delivering sustainable growth, because over time the market rewards growth and quality above everything else,” Irani said.

title: Worst Samvat under Modi era; Nifty down 13% as investors enter new year amid growing caution
